A new AD/CVD investigation was opened in May 2025 against Angola, Australia, Laos, Norway, and Thailand for the two lower grades of mg-Si (U.S. International Trade Administration 2025a). A Section 301 tariff of 50% applies to mg-Si of greater than 4N purity from China (U.S. Trade Representative 2025). All silica-based products from China’s Xinjiang region are banned by the UFLPA (U.S. Customs and Border Protection 2021; U.S. Department of Homeland Security 2022). 2.7.4 Regional Pricing for Metallurgical-Grade Silicon Ferroglobe reported that the U.S. average spot price for mg-Si was $3.97/kg in 2024 (Figure 32) (U.S. Geological Survey 2025t). Import customs value totaled $417 million in 2024 for approximately 130 kt, indicating an average import price of $3.21/kg, and a range of $2.32– $3.40/kg, depending on country of origin. Chinese mg-Si prices in early 2025 averaged $1.31/kg, while the European Union average spot price in 2024 was $2.72/kg (Ferroglobe 2025). 44 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 32. Spot prices of mg-Si in 2024. Source: (Ferroglobe 2025) 2.7.5 Upstream Inputs for Metallurgical-Grade Silicon This section provides limited information on priority mg-Si inputs. Many upstream inputs are not discussed here due to limited supply chain information or relatively low importance. • Quartz(ite): Also known as vein quartz, lump quartz, or quartz gravel. For PV applications, mg-Si needs low-impurity quartz (Brown 2018), which is typically mined as a rock and then crushed to 20–120 mm sand (Goodin 2025). This is different from the low-iron silica sand used in PV glass (see Section 2.8.5). While U.S. mg-Si is made from high-purity quartz sand, upgraded industrial-grade sand can be used for mg-Si with enough purification steps (Heidari and Anctil 2022). There may be competition for low- iron silica between mg-Si and PV glass production, but differing purity requirements and low levels of U.S. PV glass production reduce this risk. • Coke, coal, wet woodchips: These materials—readily available in the United States— provide carbon in the carbothermic reduction process of turning silicon dioxide (silica quartz sand) into mg-Si and carbon dioxide. If alternate technologies were pursued, such as hydrogen reduction of silica, demand for these materials would decrease. • Graphite electrodes: Graphite electrodes—made from needle coke and pitch (coal derivatives) then formed and baked into large rods—are consumed in the EAF during mg-Si production (GrafTech 2025). Excluding China, the world has about 786 kt of graphite electrode manufacturing capacity, which is higher than global demand (GrafTech 2025).
